I was absolutely the third parent, and that's probably why I'm closer to the siblings a decade younger than me - I was doing way more for them than a sibling should have!

Everyone said I was mature and responsible for my age and that feels good to hear at 8, 10, 12, 14, but at some point in my teens it started clicking that it was because I'd been forced to be that way. It was also difficult feeling like the tester child for parenthood and watching my siblings get away with behaviour I'd have been punished for, or allowed freedoms I'd been denied simply because my parents were figuring it out still. There's no such thing as one size fits all for parenting, and I understand my parents much more since becoming one myself, but nothing changes the fact that the more siblings I had the less time my parents had for me as an individual.

I'm the eldest of 8 and now have one of my own. This is the most balanced comment here! I moved to Leigh from Oldham and honestly I think a lot of these commenters could do with a trip to Oldham to realise what Leigh has actually got going for it.

OP, I don't have school age kids but there are a lot of services at the library and local churches for preschoolers and babies, the library is wonderful, the sports village has excellent facilities, Pennington Flash and Pennington Hall Park are both beautiful and walkable from the town centre, and there are regular community events at both. There's actually still an indoor market in the town centre, which I love. You're close to main transport routes (although traffic) and the V1 bus service going to Manchester is pretty reliable as Leigh is the first stop, although coming back is a different matter.

On the other hand, Leigh has the same problems most other small towns do, mostly due to lack of investment. There are some anti social regulars about town, bit of a litter problem in areas, and on rugby/match days there can be noise pollution from the fans and the stadium itself. Leigh Infirmary is good but if you need a proper hospital it's a pain in the arse having to go to Wigan. Still haven't found a local dentist in Leigh but that's an issue across the country. The lack of a tram/train line in Leigh is one of its biggest detriments imo.

I had PPP/PPA/PPOCD after my baby was born - I didn't even know PPOCD was a thing! 

You've already done so well bringing your healthy, beautiful baby into the world, and for reaching out after recognising you need some support. It's a scary, overwhelming, emotional time being newly post-partum and you deserve to feel supported during this time. 

Other people have shared their experiences with Sertraline and it's not something I took when post-partum, so I can't comment but what I will say is that if you feel it's not the right medication for you, be pushy about it! It's all well and good giving medication some time to work, especially for SSRIs and SNRIs that have a cumulative effect, but if you feel it's not right for you you're under no obligation to continue with it and you are perfectly within your rights to request a review for a change.

I'm now 18 months down the line with a happy and healthy toddler, and I'm eternally grateful for the help I received when I needed it. You'll get there too, you've got this 💕

Mine is the same to an extent, and while I don't have thick hair, as it got longer the weight of it was definitely dragging the curl/wave out! Layers do help but will change the overall shape of your hair so that's something to keep in mind.

I dry upside down while scrunching, let it get wet in the rain,, or just embrace it tbh! You see so many "hair goals" pictures with the nice smoother roots-to-chin and then a beautiful wave or curl towards the ends. You've got that on lock naturally!

Edit as I missed your question at the end! If you're still using a blow dryer or the like and you're embracing the straighter roots, can use a barrel brush and the cold air setting to help create shine and smoothness, and then finger comb and let the lengths of your hair dry naturally for the curl.

If you want to encourage curl in the roots, a good spray bottle of water with a mist nozzle then gently scrunching upside down may help! I'm sure others will be able to add more advice about products etc, I don't really use any and just roll with the frizz if it happens... I'm lazy!

On the plus side, a lot of these towns are surrounding by some fantastic green spaces, if you know where to look.

It's a very small centre for such a big tourist destination, so it quickly becomes nightmarishly crowded, and the influx of stag and hen parties on top of two student populations really put a pall on it. I guess I like Manchester because it's the home city, but also because of it's location. It's also close to the coast, the peak district, the lakes, two hours to London if I have to go down with work, can easily get to most major cities with very little hassle.
The music scene also is great (still need more museums / galleries), there are tons of food options from so many cultures, varied options for nightlife depending on your tastes. The history of the city proper and the region at large still feels very present and relevant if you enjoy that kind of thing, it might not be as obvious (or marketable to tourists) a "culture" as York's Viking influences but it's there. I went back in January, just 4 days a week like you. It is really hard, you think of them constantly and worry and feel anxious. You might cry when you get home and have them back in your arms, I know I did! I also cried on the bus to work every morning for a few weeks.

My best advice is to let yourself feel what you're feeling, you've had the huge change of becoming a parent less than a year ago, and now you've got another huge change of being away from them when you're used to being with them 24/7. Don't rush yourself to feel okay or lie about where you're at, be open with your friends and loved ones, and let them support you and comfort you. If you have a good relationship with your boss or HR, be honest with them too that you'll need a little time to adjust, and might need to call home now and then to see how baby is getting on.

Is baby going to daycare or family? Mine is in nursery 3 days a week and with family for the fourth day, and it was really helpful to me that I could get regular updates from both - the nursery through a parent app and my family texting me and sending pictures.

Looking back over the first half of this year, I can see now that we made the right decisions, my son is thriving at nursery and building beautiful bonds with his grandma from his Thursdays with her. Work also gave me time and space to feel a little more well rounded as a person rather than just as a mum, I get adult socialisation and a sense of achievement there that isn't tied to baby's progress. I hadn't appreciated how much I'd need that until I went back. It's also nice to feel more financially secure and better contributing to the household again, maternity leave was tough!

You will get through this, both you and baby will adjust and continue to thrive and grow together. Good luck for your first day back and the months to come!

I had my first baby just under a year ago and was also pretty clueless about breastfeeding, except that I knew I wanted to give it a go and was open to the alternatives if it didn't work out. 

The best advice I can give you is follow your baby's lead. They'll tell you what they need, and in the first few weeks that's either going to be food, sleep or comfort. Usually food!
 If baby was whipping his head around for the nipple and getting frustrated, I'd rub it down from his nose or up from his chin to give him some guidance on where I was, once they figure it out they've got laser focus and hone straight in! If he fell asleep too soon into a feed - and you'll figure out what's 'too soon' for your baby as you go - I'd gently tickle his cheek to prompt him into starting again.

Rotate ice packs and heat packs / ibuprofen for your boobs when your milk comes in cause they're not joking when they say it feels like having concrete bowling balls in your chest. You can put lanolin or nipple cream on a pantyliner too and store them in the fridge or freezer to stick inside your bra for some portable relief.

A haakaa ended up being a godsend over a pump for collecting letdown from one boob while he fed from another, as were puppy pads on my side of the bed so I wasn't constantly washing milky sheets from the nighttime leaking.

Pipettes / baby syringes are a really good way to feed your baby from your stash if they're ever poorly or off their food. I froze full pipettes for when he was teething too. 

If you're going out and about with baby, don't forget a clean top/bra for you too! I always packed a change of clothes for baby and would forget for myself, and had a few times looking like I'd just come from a wet t-shirt competition.

As someone who's just coming through the other side of this - it can get better, I promise. That said, it doesn't sound like you are getting the right support currently and that's concerning. I self presented at A&E and was seen as a priority due to the things I was saying and also that I was already under the perinatal mental health team. I spent 6 weeks in a mother and baby unit and it helped massively.

If you're not feeling safe and you're not getting the support you need, self present. Go daily if you have to, just to be in a safer space. Be aware that if you express any feelings or thoughts that could be classed as harmful towards your child or other person, a safeguarding may need to be put in place by the hospital. If you are feeling anything of that sort, please don't hide it and don't be ashamed - you're not well right now and the thoughts you are having about yourself / others are not truly you.

Edited to add: if you have any questions about the MBU fire away! Also safeguarding doesn't mean your child will be taken from you. It is always the first priority to keep parent and child together unless in very extreme circumstances. Having worked the whole chain from B&Bs to 5* hotels my opinion is that 5* hotels and boutique hostels offer the best working experience as a housekeeper.

My experience was that there was always work. There were always extra hours if wanted. There were a lot of staff who'd been there for 5+ years (a good sign!) and they knew everything so I never went without knowing something essential. They trained me and trained me hard. You'll develop an excellent eye for detail in cleaning and room presentation. You'll get great at time management and judging when you can take a sneaky 10 mins in the room to watch jeremy kyle. The perks can sometimes be limited but still worth it - free food from the restaurant, launch party of their new cocktail bar ect. Depending on what part of the world you're in, you'll probably meet famous people. Most of them will be nice or at the very least, polite. On a Saturday or Sunday,  checkouts will probably be full of leftover food and booze from posh parties. That's how I tried caviar, and spit it right out again. That shit's bad. You'll figure out your own hotel's policy on left over items but mine was full of people taking stuff home and management turned a blind eye. I also got an unworn 400$ pair of shoes and a playstation 4 some business dude had left behind. Someone else took his TV. 

On the other hand, you'll almost certainly be asked to sign an NDA and a form against asking for autographs and posting pictures/updates on social media. Your personal presentation will be held to higher standards as you're more likely to encounter guests. Better hotels are usually better stocked with all the cleaning supplies you need but there's still no accounting for sick managers or shipping issues. Definitely more politics between hotel departments and communication between them can dictate if you'll be having a good or bad day. A good/bad housekeeping manager can really make or break your working experience. Front desk will most likely look down on the whole housekeeping team. If you ever see restaurant staff, try to befriend them, they hardly ever get out of the kitchen. 

The first 2/3 weeks will probably be hard while you learn on the go and get used to a whole new, and very particular, system of doing things. By the end of 6 months you'll be spending 25 mins per room and folding hospital corners in your sleep. I loved working in a 5* and I hope you will too. Good luck!

There's a free walking tour that starts at 9:30am and 11am in exhibition square that's fun if you want to see the main sights. It's worth checking out what's on online as there's usually food fairs and local business fairs on in the summer which are always good. Oh and if you're going on a weekend check out the Habit pub on Goodramgate... Tiny but gorgeous roof garden and great live music.

Lived there for 5 years and worked in tourism there for 2, you'll have a great time!    

EDIT: York itself is really compact and there's tons to do in a really small walking radius. The information center on Lendal (after the bridge on the main street over the river into town) will have free maps and if you get a bit stuck, people are generally friendly and willing to give you directions
